S033.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
S033.description: A distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood.

subtypes.Elevated Mood: A mood that is abnormally high, euphoric, and full of unmotivated happiness and vitality.
subtypes.Irritable Mood: A state where one gets angry or aggressive even at minor stimuli.
subtypes.Mood Lability: Rapid shifts in mood, alternating unpredictably between euphoria and irritability.

S034.name: Increased_Activity
S034.description: Abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy.

subtypes.Increased Energy: Overflowing physical and mental energy, leading to an inability to stay still and a desire to keep moving.
subtypes.Hyperactivity: Doing far more work than usual or starting multiple activities simultaneously.
subtypes.Psychomotor Agitation: Inability to tolerate resting or stopping, driven by a constant need to do something.

S035.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
S035.description: Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity (may range from uncritical self-confidence to delusional proportions).

subtypes.Inflated Self-Confidence: Feeling capable of anything and believing that failure is impossible, unlike one's usual self.
subtypes.Overestimation of Abilities: Unrealistically assessing one's talents, knowledge, or abilities as superior.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one is a special and important person with a special mission or purpose.

S036.name: Decreased_Sleep
S036.description: Decreased need for sleep (e.g., feels rested after only 3 hours of sleep).

subtypes.Reduced Sleep Duration: Sleeping significantly less than usual but feeling refreshed rather than tired.
subtypes.Loss of Sleep Need: Not feeling the urge to sleep or the thought that sleep is necessary.
subtypes.Indifference to Insomnia: Feeling no problem and continuing activities despite staying up for several nights.

S039.name: Manic_Distractibility
S039.description: Attention is too easily drawn to unimportant or irrelevant external stimuli.

subtypes.Responsiveness to Extraneous Stimuli: Attention is immediately drawn to trivial and unimportant stimuli nearby (e.g., noise, movement).
subtypes.Frequent Task Switching: Unable to finish one task and constantly shifting attention to new things, starting multiple tasks simultaneously.
subtypes.Inability to Sustain Attention: Unable to focus on any activity for long, with attention constantly being scattered.

symptom.disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder is characterized by at least one lifetime manic episode, often accompanied by depressive episodes, with mood and energy changes that are clearly distinct from the person's usual functioning and cause marked impairment or require hospitalization. Manic episodes typically involve persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased goal-directed activity or energy lasting at least one week, though episodes can last months if untreated. The course is usually recurrent, with episodes triggered or unmasked by stressors, sleep disruption, or substance use, but not solely caused by them. It is distinguished from Bipolar II by the presence of full mania (rather than hypomania) and from unipolar depression or primary psychotic disorders by the cyclical pattern of mood elevation and depression and the temporal relationship between mood and psychotic features when present.

patient.stressor: Martha’s episode developed during a high-stakes year when she secured a major grant and was promoted to lead a new condensed matter lab, coinciding with a heavy teaching load and several grant deadlines. At first, colleagues saw her as simply energized and productive, staying late to run experiments and sending an unusual volume of late-night emails, but over several months her intensity escalated as she proposed multiple new projects, demanded round-the-clock availability from students, and began rewriting approved protocols on the fly. Her meticulous planning gave way to chaotic, overambitious commitments: she volunteered to organize a regional conference, agreed to extra committee work, and insisted on reanalyzing years’ worth of data, leading to missed deadlines, complaints from graduate students, and concern from department leadership about her increasingly volatile meetings. After a tense faculty review where she reacted angrily to feedback and her partner at home reported that she hadn’t been sleeping and seemed uncharacteristically “amped up” and distractible, her department chair privately suggested she see occupational health, which then referred her for psychiatric evaluation when it became clear her work and relationships were significantly impaired.
patient.chief_complaint: “For months I’ve felt unusually ‘up’ and on edge all the time, like my mood is cranked way higher than normal and I can’t dial it back.”

S033.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
S033.description: A distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood.
S033.manifestation: Lately it’s like someone wired me to a constant high voltage—I'm either euphoric and talking a mile a minute about my ideas, or I flip on a dime and snap at my students or my partner over tiny things, and I just can’t seem to bring the dial back to normal.

S034.name: Increased_Activity
S034.description: Abnormally and persistently increased goal-directed activity or energy.
S034.manifestation: For months I've been bouncing from the lab to my office to committee meetings, starting new experiments, drafting conference proposals, rewriting lectures all night, and I literally can’t sit still long enough to finish anything before I feel compelled to jump into the next ‘big’ thing.

S035.name: Inflated_Self_Esteem
S035.description: Inflated self-esteem or grandiosity (may range from uncritical self-confidence to delusional proportions).
S035.manifestation: I’ve been absolutely convinced that I’m on the verge of a field‑changing breakthrough, that only I can see the connections everyone else is missing, and when colleagues question me it feels ridiculous because in my mind there’s no doubt I’m operating on a different level than they are.

S036.name: Decreased_Sleep
S036.description: Decreased need for sleep (e.g., feels rested after only 3 hours of sleep).
S036.manifestation: Most nights I only sleep two or three hours, if that, but I wake up buzzing with ideas, pacing around making notes on the whiteboard at 3 a.m., and I don’t feel tired at all, just irritated that my body can’t keep up with how fast my mind is going.

S039.name: Manic_Distractibility
S039.description: Attention is too easily drawn to unimportant or irrelevant external stimuli.
S039.manifestation: In meetings or in the lab my mind jumps everywhere—an email ping, a flickering light, a random thought about a new grant idea—and I suddenly abandon what I was doing to chase that distraction, so I have half‑finished notes, experiments, and conversations scattered all over the place.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: Over the past several months my lab has slipped into chaos—deadlines have been missed, students have complained to the department about my erratic behavior, and my chair has warned that my promotion and even my position could be at risk, while at home my partner is exhausted and says I’m impossible to be around.
add_requirements.duration: These problems have been building for about seven months now, basically since I got the big grant and took over the new lab and everything started ramping up.
